sentences.text: Thalassodromeus possessed one of the largest known pterosaur skulls, measuring around 1.42 meters in length, and one of the largest cranial crests of any vertebrate.
Although only the skull is known, Thalassodromeus is estimated to have had a wingspan between 4.2 and 4.5 meters.
Although incomplete, the total length of the lower jaw of Thalassodromeus sethi is estimated at 670 millimeters.
The mandibular symphysis occupied 47 percent of the lower jaw's total length.
A lower jaw fragment attributed to Thalassodromeus suggests an individual with a wingspan of 5.3 meters.
The genus Thalassodromeus was described by Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos in 2002.
The original skull of Thalassodromeus was discovered in 1983 in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil.
The first known specimen of Thalassodromeus was collected in 1983 near Santana do Cariri in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil.
The concave palatine bones of Thalassodromeus were hypothesized to help the animal momentarily store food while skimming.
A 2015 study by Pêgas and Kellner indicated that Thalassodromeus sethi had a strong bite force based on its well-developed jaw muscles.
Witton hypothesized that the crest was inflatable with blood to act like a fan, helping change head attitude during flight and water contact without requiring powerful neck muscles.
Witton suggested that thalassodromids had terrestrial abilities comparable to azhdarchids due to similar limb proportions.
Thalassodromids likely had limbs capable of long strides, with short, compact feet making these mechanics efficient.
Witton cautioned that more analysis was needed to confirm the terrestrial abilities of thalassodromids.
Researchers Kellner and Campos originally classified Thalassodromeus in the family Tapejaridae due to its large crest and large nasoantorbital fenestra.
In 2006, Martill and Naish argued that Tapejaridae was an unnatural group and placed Thalassodromeus as a sister taxon to the family Azhdarchidae.
While Kellner classified Thalassodromeus in the family Tapejaridae, other analyses place it in the group Thalassodrominae, closer to the family Azhdarchidae.
The genus authority for Thalassodromeus is Kellner & Campos, 2002.
The only known species of Thalassodromeus is T. sethi, described by Kellner & Campos in 2002.
Thalassodromeus lived approximately 110 million years ago during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous period.
The environment where Thalassodromeus lived had a tropical climate similar to modern-day Brazil.
Thalassodromeus lived approximately between 122 and 109 million years ago.
Thalassodromeus is known from the Romualdo Formation, where it coexisted with other pterosaurs, dinosaurs, and animals.
The Paleobiology Database records the time range of Thalassodromeus as the Aptian stage, from 119.57 to 113.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether the crest of Thalassodromeus served functions like thermoregulation and display, though it likely had multiple functions.
In 2006, David M. Martill and Darren Naish suggested that Thalassodromeus was a junior synonym of Tupuxuara, a theory later rejected by Kellner and Campos.
In 2015, Jaime A. Headden and Herbert B. N. Campos described the jaw tip of Thalassodromeus as a new genus, Banguela oberlii, interpreting it as a toothless dsungaripterid.
In 2020, James McPhee and colleagues argued that Banguela was a valid genus belonging to the family Chaoyangopteridae rather than a dsungaripterid.
The classification of Thalassodromeus and its relatives remains one of the most contentious issues in pterosaur research.
Martill and Naish suggested the crest developed late in life and was likely related to sexual display, with maturity assessable by crest size.
The function of Thalassodromeus's crest is unknown, though it may have been used for sexual display, species recognition, or thermoregulation.
